14151523f16b3513: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 20 — There is something immediately comforting about a plate of grilled chicken.
The way you become aware of it before it even appears at your table: the warm, woodsy scent of rosemary; the clear, citrusy hint of lemon.
It comes with a generous serve of creamy mashed potatoes, alongside broccoli and cherry tomatoes that add a welcome freshness and bite.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The lemon-centric décor of Taman Desa’s Lemon Sole Café.
The chicken itself is tender and well seasoned, while the lemon cuts through the richness of the potatoes, preventing the whole dish from feeling too heavy.
Unfussy and satisfying, I enjoyed this at Lemon Sole Café, a new casual dining restaurant in Taman Desa.
Opened less than six months ago, Lemon Sole has already attracted a steady clientele of neighbourhood residents who enjoy hearty, unpretentious Asian and Western fusion fare.
Consider it Taman Desa’s latest soul food sanctuary.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Americano, iced and hot.
The name is especially fitting given the profusion of lemons throughout the space, from the striking mural of lemons and lemon blossoms on the feature wall to their use as a seasoning in some dishes.
Which makes it a no-brainer to order the aforementioned rosemary infused lemon chicken. What else on the “something for everyone” menu seems tempting?
Perhaps the ayam percik poke bowl? Or the chicken karaage buttermilk fettuccine?
Choices, choices. But first, something to drink.
We kept it minimalist with our beverages: Americanos, both iced and hot. The better to keep our palate clean and taste the flavours, possibly. Or, you know, because we needed the caffeine.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Nasi lemak with ayam rendang.

Whatever the reason, black coffee helps to keep our wits sharp and the conversation flowing. There is an ease in falling back to old patterns, catching up with our lives, sharing triumphs and tribulations equally, whether minor or major.
Life is connection, after all. It’s that simple, really.
The Americano cuts through the richness of the mashed potatoes, which in turn provides a soft, starchy bed for each bite of the lemony grilled chicken. Comforting.

For something more local, the restaurant also offers their signature nasi lemak with either breaded chicken or ayam rendang. We opted for the latter, naturally, in favour of a more complete Malaysian flavour.

The coconut milk infused rice grains are fluffy and fragrant; the chunks of chicken generously sized and tender. More crucially, for fastidious fans of nasi lemak, the fried ikan bilis and peanuts are fresh and crunchy.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
All-day breakfast.

Fancy a little bit of everything? Lemon Sole also offers a classic all day breakfast. Expect baked beans and hash browns, sausages and sourdough. A fresh salad balanced with sautéed mushrooms and blistered cherry tomatoes.

Ultimately the food at Lemon Sole is a bit of East meets West — from the Japanese katsu curry to the pesto crusted seared seabass — with plenty of fusion choices along the way. (The bunga kantan aglio olio, for instance, sounds promising.)
Yet for all the variety in the menu, it is perhaps the convivial, community-centric ambience that is what stays with you long after you have paid your bill.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Red bean soup.
The friendly and helpful servers; the cheeriness of the citrus-accented décor; that sense of home and hospitality bundled in one cosy dining experience.
The latter is best exemplified by the unexpected complimentary bowls of tong sui — sweet red bean soup — which delights the Cantonese in me. A small gesture, sure, but heartwarming all the same.
And in these trying times, every bit of kindness helps.
Lemon Sole Café
45, Jalan 2/109E,
Taman Desa Business Park, KL.
Open daily (except Mon closed) 9 am–9 pm
IG: https://www.instagram.com/lemonsolecafe/

cee4013ba2e05bb0: LISBON, Oct 20 — Cristiano Ronaldo has been handed a 30-day suspension for leaving the Portuguese national team camp, the country’s football federation (FPF) announced on Monday.
The 41-year-old abruptly left the Portugal camp on September 30 during the Uefa Nations League, before accusing coach Jorge Jesus of breaking his word about giving him game time.
Ronaldo apologised to supporters earlier in October, adding he would accept any punishment that was imposed.

The former Manchester United and Real Madrid star, who will also have to pay a fine of 255 euros (RM1,168), has received the minimum penalty provided for in the federation’s regulations, which stipulate suspensions of between one and six months for leaving the national team.

Ronaldo left Portugal’s squad after first being made to warm up as a substitute against Norway on September 27 and not being brought on, and then finding out he would not start against Denmark in the match on October 1.
Ronaldo’s suspension takes effect from the day of the Denmark match, meaning he has already served 19 days of his ban and will complete it by the end of October.

The FPF disciplinary committee said it took into account “the remorse shown in the statement” issued by Ronaldo on October 6, in which he admitted his mistake and expressed his willingness to accept a punishment.
The five-time Ballon d’Or winner is Portugal’s all-time top goalscorer and record appearance-maker in men’s international football.
But in his absence, Portugal won all four of their Nations League matches and qualified for the quarter-finals with two games to spare.
Portugal host Denmark on November 14 and then travel to face Wales on November 17 in their final two Nations League Group A4 matches — by which time Ronaldo will have served his suspension.

In a social media post shortly after his walk-out, Ronaldo accused Portugal boss Jesus of breaking his word about giving him game time in Nations League matches but insisted he was not retiring from international duty.
“I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team,” Ronaldo posted.

He said Jesus had gone back on his word about bringing him on against Norway, and then in a press conference before the Denmark match had not said a series of points they had agreed upon during a conversation beforehand.
One of Ronaldo’s pre-approved talking points was that Jesus had “made a mistake in asking someone of the stature of Pele or Maradona to warm up and then not sending him on in the match”.
Jesus, speaking several days later, said he would select Ronaldo for international duty if the forward was playing for his club Al Nassr, and was interested in being called up.

Following the FPF’s announcement, Ronaldo did not directly react to the news on Instagram but did post a picture of himself preparing to train with his Saudi club, accompanied with the caption, “Putting in the work”. — AFP

77b09e5fdb9ce990: KUALA LANGAT: Syahidatul Azimah Azmi, who once collected coins with her husband to buy rice and petrol, was moved to tears when he surprised her with a Mitsubishi XForce.

According to Harian Metro, Syahidatul, 34, said the gift from her husband, Abubakar Sanusi, 30, reminded her of how far they had come since tying the knot in September 2016, and of the challenges they had overcome together.

She said she had never expected to receive the Mitsubishi XForce, as their Proton Persona, which they had used since 2012, before their marriage, had become increasingly prone to breakdowns, making daily travel difficult.
"I only asked my husband for a Perodua Axia, as long as I had a vehicle that was easy to use to get around," she said.
The couple met at Madrasah Syeikhul Ariffien in Melaka, where Syahidatul worked and Abubakar was a student.
They decided to marry after three months of getting to know each other seriously.
Although both came from financially comfortable families, they chose to build a life of their own after marriage.

Syahidatul said their limited income in the early years meant they had to be careful with their spending, as Abubakar was training as a car mechanic on a monthly allowance of RM250 while she earned RM1,000.
"Our limited income meant we had to be frugal to meet all our commitments. There was a point when we had to collect coins to buy petrol and rice," she said.
Despite their struggles, the couple remained determined to improve their circumstances.
Abubakar now runs a car workshop in Bandar Saujana Putra, enabling them to enjoy a more stable life.
Syahidatul said the Mitsubishi XForce left her surprised and emotional, as it reminded her of their journey from struggling to afford basic necessities to enjoying a more comfortable life.
"When I think about it, we have come a long way, from trying to scrape together enough money to buy rice and petrol to where we are today.
"It's not just about the car. Looking back at our journey since the beginning of our marriage, we have been through so much together.
"Alhamdulillah, I am grateful for what we have today," she said.

Two people who were inside the unit were evacuated by SCDF, with one taken to Singapore General Hospital (SGH) for smoke inhalation.
A person from a neighbouring unit was also taken to SGH for smoke inhalation.
About 25 people were evacuated by the police and SCDF as a precautionary measure, while the cause of the fire remains under investigation.
AsiaOne has reached out to the police for comment. — AsiaOne

2e75b8b223d6a17a: OCTOBER 20 — I remember standing by the water in Pasir Gudang, looking towards the horizon and wondering how far the world really went.
There were ships in the distance, some moving slowly while others seemed to be waiting for their turn at the busy port.
Across the water was Singapore, or at least that was what I imagined I was looking at. I could never be entirely sure which buildings belonged to which part of the shoreline, but it hardly mattered.
There was so much happening out there, and to a boy growing up in Pontian, the whole scene seemed wonderfully alive.

We were actually in Pasir Gudang to visit Abah’s youngest sister and her family, who lived there. It was one of those family visits that formed part of growing up, with Mak driving us in our secondhand Honda hatchback.
Watching the ships was simply something we took the opportunity to do while we were there. After all, what else was there for a boy to look at in a port town?
Pontian was also a coastal town, although not quite in the way people usually imagine seaside places.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Watching the ships was simply something we took the opportunity to do while we were there. — Picture from https://www.expedia.com/
We had the sea, certainly, but much of our coastline was lined with mangrove forests rather than sandy beaches.
The water was familiar to us, yet it never quite offered the same spectacle as the busy port at Pasir Gudang.
Watching those ships made me feel that there was an enormous world beyond the places I knew, filled with people travelling somewhere and carrying things from places I had never heard of.
Mak was the one who drove us there.
We had a secondhand Honda hatchback, which served as our family car during those years.
I cannot remember how often we made those outings, or whether they followed any particular routine.

What I remember is the excitement of going somewhere different, sitting in the car with my brothers and watching the familiar roads give way to places we rarely visited. Even the journey felt like part of the adventure.
As children, we never thought very much about what it took to make those trips possible.
We knew the car was not new, but that hardly mattered. It could take us places, and Mak knew how to drive it.

Petrol was something adults worried about, just as they worried about whether the car needed servicing or whether there was enough money for the coming week. We were mostly concerned with where we were going and how long it would take to get there.

Looking back, I realise that our childhood was lived within fairly modest means. Abah was a teacher, and Mak managed the household with the kind of careful attention that becomes necessary when there are seven children to raise.

There were bills to pay, school expenses to consider and groceries to buy. Money had to be stretched, and I suspect there were many decisions made around the household budget that never reached our ears.
Our meals were similarly ordinary. Fish and eggs appeared regularly on the table, while chicken and beef were more closely associated with occasions such as Hari Raya.

We ate what was available, and Mak made sure there was enough for everyone. I do not remember sitting at the table thinking that something was missing simply because another family might have been eating something different.
That is perhaps the part I find most interesting now. We did not feel poor.
I do not mean that we had everything we wanted, or that there were never things we wished we could afford.
Like most children, we probably asked for more than our parents could reasonably provide. But when I think about those years, the memories that return are not primarily about what we lacked.
They are about the things we did together, the places we visited and the ordinary routines that made our little world feel complete.
It would be easy, of course, to turn those memories into a romantic story about growing up with very little. I would rather not.
Financial limitations are real, and there is nothing particularly charming about having to calculate whether there is enough money for petrol or groceries.
Mak and Abah had to make those calculations, even when we children were happily occupied with something else.
What seemed like an ordinary visit to relatives has remained with me for decades, not because anything remarkable happened, but because of how the world looked to me then.
Mak was simply taking us to see family. I was discovering that there was so much more of the world I had yet to see.
Since Mak passed away last month, I have found myself returning to memories like this more often.
Not necessarily the important occasions that everyone remembers, but the ordinary days that somehow survived in my mind for decades.
I wish I could ask her what she remembered about those trips, whether she enjoyed watching the ships too, or whether she was already thinking about the journey home and the petrol left in the tank.
I suppose I will never know. What I do know is that she gave us a childhood in which the world seemed much larger than our circumstances.
We were not unaware that money mattered, but we were allowed to be children without carrying every worry that came with it.
And when I think of that boy standing by the water in Pasir Gudang, imagining Singapore somewhere beyond the ships, I remember how enormous the world appeared to him.
Only now do I appreciate how much Mak had already done to let him see it.

b159883b70efb5df: PUTRAJAYA: The Registrar of Societies Malaysia (RoS) has confirmed that Perikatan Nasional's registration has been cancelled, saying the coalition's explanation failed to address the grounds for cancellation outlined in an earlier notice.
RoS said the decision was made under subparagraph 13(1)(c)(iv) of the Societies Act 1966 (Act 832), after reviewing all documents and representations submitted by PN on Oct 12.
It said a notice dated Sept 22 had been issued to PN under subsection 13(2) of the Act, allowing the coalition to provide explanations and representations on the matters raised.
"After reviewing all documents and explanations submitted, the Registrar of Societies found that the reasons given failed to refute the grounds for cancellation of registration stated in the notice.
"They also did not provide sufficient justification to maintain the organisation's registration," it said.
ba99267112791300: YANGON, Oct 20 — Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi received a package from Britain’s King Charles III on Monday, authorities said, releasing the first pictures of the detained Nobel laureate in two months and describing her as a “special female prisoner”.

It is the first time Myanmar authorities have used the term to describe Suu Kyi, who was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED.

The coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April following elections that did not include Suu Kyi’s party, and she was moved to house arrest soon afterwards.

Home ministry officials met her on Monday to deliver a package of two books about soil, “one sealed envelope, and a sealed diplomatic communication sent by King Charles III of the United Kingdom to the special female detainee”, Myanmar’s presidential spokeswoman said on her Facebook page.
Britain is Myanmar’s former colonial power and the monarch is known to have a keen interest in gardening and the environment.
Accompanying the statement were two images of Suu Kyi meeting two men with their backs to the camera.

The pictures appeared to be in a similar room to the last released images of her, when she met a Red Cross representative in August, her first publicised meeting with a foreign official since her ouster.
Fact-checkers from AFP examined the latest photos and found no evidence of manipulation using Meta Generative AI or OpenAI tools.
Suu Kyi remains detained on charges rights groups say were concocted to return power to the military, which has historically ruled Myanmar since independence.
“I have been extremely lenient toward her,” Min Aung Hlaing said in an interview with Time magazine published last month.
In response to questions from AFP the Foreign Office in London did not say whether British diplomats had sought to deliver the package in person, or been refused permission to do so.
Britain condemns what it describes as Suu Kyi’s “arbitrary detention” and calls for her immediate and unconditional release. — AFP
e70150d1cff6f25d: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia has made no agreement or commitment to provide financial assistance to budget airline operator AirAsia, the finance ministry said, though it acknowledged concerns over the carrier's financial health following a jump in jet fuel prices.

Reuters reported this month, citing sources, that AirAsia was in talks with the government over potential support. The airline's co-founder Tony Fernandes said the talks focused on aviation-related costs such as airport charges and fuel, not financial assistance.

In a written parliamentary reply on Monday, the finance ministry said it was monitoring developments in Malaysia's aviation sector, including recent quarterly losses reported by AirAsia that were attributed to rising fuel costs stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran.

The government was regularly engaging with aviation players and seeking views from industry and technical experts, as was the case for other economic sectors affected by the Middle East crisis, it said.

Any request for support from companies in any sector "will be considered based on the interests of the country and the people, the fiscal sustainability of the government and the protection of public funds, in accordance with applicable laws and procedures," the ministry said.
"To date, the government has not made any agreement or commitment to provide financing support to AirAsia, whether in the form of guarantees, loans or public fund injections," it said.

The ministry said AirAsia was a significant player in the aviation sector, accounting for around 41 per cent of the 104.5 million passenger movements recorded at airports operated by Malaysia Airports Holdings in 2025 and almost 60 per cent of domestic passenger movements.
The carrier also played a significant role in maintaining air connectivity in Malaysia's Sabah and Sarawak states on Borneo Island, it said.
07aa4d807a7d44f4: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's plantation sector could receive a timely boost if the government waives crude palm oil (CPO) export tax to help clear swelling inventories, restore export competitiveness and claw back market share from Indonesia.

According to a wires report, the government is considering the proposal amid an oversupply situation, with the Plantation and Commodities Ministry expected to discuss the matter with industry players today.

Public Investment Bank (PublicInvest) analyst Chong Hoe Leong believes the proposed waiver could benefit upstream plantation companies by making Malaysian palm oil more competitive in international markets, particularly as Indonesia's exports gain ground while Malaysia grapples with mounting inventories.
"We believe the proposal would be well received and likely will take effect soon. The waiver of CPO export tax will help Malaysia regain market share from Indonesia," he said in a note.
Malaysia's CPO inventory reached a record 3.5 million tonnes last month, reflecting the pressure on exporters from the price gap between Malaysian and Indonesian palm oil.

At the current 10 per cent CPO export tax rate in Malaysia, compared with Indonesia's combined export duty and levy of US$273 per tonne (RM1,113 per tonne), Indonesian CPO has been trading at a discount of RM700 to RM900 per tonne against Malaysian prices.

"This wide discount has put Malaysia's CPO exporters at a disadvantage, resulting in a significant loss of market share to our counterparts and a record inventory level of 3.5 million tonnes last month.
"This is evident as Indonesian palm oil exports have grown, in contrast to Malaysia's lacklustre performance," Chong said.
The price differential has put Malaysian exporters at a disadvantage, contributing to weaker export performance and allowing Indonesia to capture a larger share of the global market.
A waiver could narrow the competitiveness gap and provide relief to local exporters, particularly following India's reduction of its CPO import tax to five per cent from 10 per cent.
Malaysia previously waived CPO export tax for six months in 2020.
"We suggest the CPO tax waiver should be in place until the inventory level falls below 2.0 million tonnes."
However, the benefits would not be evenly distributed across the sector.

Chnong said upstream plantation companies stand to gain from stronger demand and potentially improved selling prices, while downstream players could face margin pressure if cheaper raw materials become less readily available.

The potential policy shift comes as plantation companies prepare to report their third-quarter 2026 results, with Chong anticipating stronger earnings on the back of higher fresh fruit bunch (FFB) production, lower production costs and firmer CPO prices.

He said that all plantation companies under coverage recorded production growth, led by Ta Ann Holdings Bhd, whose output rose 30 per cent year-on-year, followed by Sarawak Plantation Bhd at 23.2 per cent and Kuala Lumpur Kepong Bhd at 16.4 per cent.
Average CPO prices also strengthened to RM4,552 per tonne in the third quarter of 2026, compared with RM4,275 per tonne a year earlier, providing further support for earnings.

Against this backdrop, Chong maintains an "Overweight" call on the plantation sector, with Sarawak Plantation and Ta Ann emerging as preferred picks for their attractive dividend yields and above-industry-average FFB production growth.

The combination of potentially stronger export competitiveness, improving production and attractive dividend yields could support the sector's performance in the second half of 2026, although the actual impact will depend on whether the government proceeds with the proposed tax waiver and how quickly inventories normalise.

d84f3b55b1f0b374: MUNICH: Champions League hopefuls Bayern Munich are set for an early test of their title credentials when they host English champions Arsenal on Wednesday without in-form winger Michael Olise.
The London-born Olise, who started in Arsenal's junior system, is suspended after picking up two yellow cards inside a minute in Bayern's 3-3 draw with Viking last week.

After seeing a first yellow for a foul, a clearly frustrated Olise responded to some verbal provocation from Viking captain Zlatko Tripic by throwing the ball at his head to be sent off for the first time in his career.
After being thrust into Ballon d'Or contention due to last season's stellar showing, the former Crystal Palace winger has continued his excellent form this campaign.
Olise has nine goals and five assists from 10 games in all competitions for Bayern.

With Jamal Musiala struggling with injury and illness and both Serge Gnabry and Lennart Karl well off their best form, Olise and the ever-reliable Harry Kane have shouldered Bayern's attacking burden so far this season.
The England captain has nine goals and six assists in 10 games. With Bayern 2-0 down away at Viking last week, Kane almost single-handedly engineered a comeback, scoring twice and setting up another.
Speaking after Bayern's ruthless 6-1 victory over RB Leipzig in the Bundesliga on Saturday, Kane said Bayern would miss Olise but called on the rest of their star-studded squad to step up.
"Missing one of your biggest players, you're going to feel it for sure, but that's where other people have to step up and show they can take their opportunity," Kane said.
"We talk about the squad a lot, we talk about being ready for your moment and whoever plays will have to be ready."
One of the many positives to come out of Saturday's thumping win over Leipzig was the performance of Luis Diaz.
The 29-year-old had cut a frustrated figure after a poor start to the season but scored three goals and set up another in one of his best performances since moving from Liverpool in 2025.
'One of the best'
Despite swapping north London for the Bavarian capital back in 2023, former Tottenham captain Kane has seen plenty of Arsenal since joining Bayern.
Bayern faced the Gunners in two quarter-final legs in 2023-24, progressing by just a goal, but were outclassed in a 3-1 defeat in the league phase of last year's competition.
With domestic and international matches coming thick and fast, Kane has not had time to exchange pleasantries with any of his Gunners rivals.

"I spoke to them a bit in the international break previously and we knew the game was coming up, but I think we're all too busy right now to text each other, with a game every three days," he explained.
Saturday's thrashing of Leipzig once again showed the perennial German champions are a cut above their domestic rivals and Kane said Bayern were relishing a chance to take on Mikel Arteta's side.
Still smarting from last year's painful loss on penalties to Paris Saint-Germain, Arsenal have started strongly, winning 10 of 11 games in all competitions.
"It's a big game and we're playing against one of the best teams in Europe, you have to always enjoy these occasions," Kane said.
"We're testing ourselves against one of the best, we're here at home, the energy, the fans, it's going to be a special night."

d3500e90eaaabfd9: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 20 — The ringgit opened mostly higher against major currencies on Tuesday despite a stronger US dollar, supported by easing domestic inflation and expectations of a possible normalisation of the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR).
Against the greenback, the ringgit strengthened to 4.0780/0850 at 8am, from Monday’s close of 4.0805/0845.
The Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) reported that inflation eased to 1.8 per cent in September 2026, from 1.9 per cent in August.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid expected the ringgit to trade within a range of RM4.07 to RM4.08 against the US dollar today.
He said investors were also monitoring geopolitical risks in West Asia after Iran’s navy reported an attack by the US military on the Konarak naval base.
“We are entering the blackout period, during which US Federal Reserve officials will not be commenting publicly ahead of next week’s Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting,” he told Bernama.
The US Dollar Index (DXY), which measures the greenback against a basket of major currencies, rose 0.15 per cent to 101.989 points, he added.

At the opening, the ringgit traded mostly higher against major currencies. It strengthened against the Japanese yen to 2.5724/5770 from 2.5790/5817 at Monday’s close, and rose against the British pound to 5.4274/4367 from 5.4369/4422.
However, it edged lower against the euro to 4.5731/5809 from 4.5726/5771 previously.
The ringgit also strengthened against most of its ASEAN peers.
It edged up against the Indonesian rupiah to 225.9/226.4 from 226.0/226.4 on Monday, and against the Philippine peso to 6.46/6.48 from 6.47/6.48.
The local currency also rose against the Singapore dollar to 3.1862/1919 from 3.1886/1920 at the previous close, and strengthened against the Thai baht to 12.1373/1661 from 12.1451/1613. — Bernama
b27b4e42bbbea1ee: OCTOBER 20 — Europe is living through a period of mounting social anxiety. Recent protests in France, Portugal and Italy have centred on housing, wages, living costs and strained public services. They were not coordinated and should not be read as a single movement, nor should peaceful mobilisation be confused with the violence of smaller groups.

Yet together they raise a question that reaches beyond Europe: what happens when an economy looks sound on paper while its citizens feel increasingly insecure? Asean has a direct stake in Europe’s stability. Asean–EU trade in goods reached €274.9 billion in 2025. But the deeper lesson concerns the relationship between economic performance and political consent. Governments cannot take public confidence for granted when improvements in national indicators fail to translate into greater security at home.

In France, anger over public services has broadened into a wider challenge over living standards. School protests over teacher shortages and deteriorating conditions spread into nationwide demonstrations over inequality, public spending and rising costs. The political difficulty is straightforward: governments measure fiscal prudence through budgets and borrowing, while families judge it partly by whether a classroom has a teacher.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Demonstrators stand amid tear gas with fired by riot police during a high-school students protest as part of a nationwide protest movement over learning conditions in Lyon on October 13, 2026. — AFP pic

This does not mean fiscal constraints can be ignored. It means that decisions about spending are also decisions about the services through which citizens experience the state. A government may improve its fiscal position while weakening public confidence if the adjustment leaves essential services visibly worse.

In Portugal, housing affordability exposes a similar gap between national economic performance and household security. Tens of thousands marched through Lisbon on October 17 against rising living costs and unaffordable housing, while protesters also established tent encampments to demand action. House prices have more than doubled since 2017, and rents on new leases have nearly doubled.

Portugal’s attraction to tourists, investors and mobile professionals has not necessarily made its cities more livable for existing residents. When housing supply fails to meet local needs and property prices outpace domestic wages, international success can deepen insecurity rather than relieve it. A city can become more attractive to the world while becoming less accessible to its own people.

In Milan, a march against war and rising living costs began peacefully before groups broke away, clashed with police and looted shops around Piazza del Duomo. Such violence should be condemned without being allowed to erase the grievances of peaceful demonstrators. Nor should the prosperity of a major financial and commercial centre be mistaken for security shared by all its residents.

External shocks are intensifying these domestic pressures. The conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran has disrupted energy supplies and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The European Union imports about 80 per cent of the gas it needs, leaving households and industry exposed to international supply disruptions and price increases. Insecurity along the Red Sea route adds risks to shipping between Asia and Europe.

These shocks did not create Europe’s housing shortages or public-service grievances. They aggravate existing strains. Higher energy and transport costs reach citizens through electricity bills, petrol prices and supermarket purchases, while governments face renewed demands for assistance. Households already struggling to cover essentials have little room to absorb another increase.

Asean is exposed to the same external pressures. The region is a net oil importer, and its petroleum-security framework recognize the importance of reliable and diversified supplies. Energy and freight disruptions can raise production costs for South-east Asian firms even as pressure on European households threatens demand for their exports.

Europe’s domestic difficulties could also complicate its external economic agenda. Governments facing demands to protect jobs and purchasing power may find some trade compromises harder to defend. But this is not an inevitable retreat: both Europe and Asean retain strong incentives to diversify markets and deepen economic ties. The practical task is to sustain cooperation while preparing for a less predictable trading environment.

The more uncomfortable lesson, however, lies within Asean itself. Europe’s predicament should not invite triumphalism. Housing affordability, insecure employment and uneven access to public services are not exclusively European concerns.

Malaysia’s housing debate illustrates the point. Local incomes and housing prices do not always align, and national averages can obscure substantial differences between places and households. A buoyant property market is not, by itself, evidence that ordinary families can afford a suitable home. Local household incomes should guide public-housing prices, while new homes should connect residents to jobs and public transport. A lower purchase price offers little relief if the savings are swallowed by commuting costs.

Household security also depends on the region’s ability to withstand external disruptions. Asean renewed its petroleum-security agreement in 2025, and member states have recently advanced cooperation on the Asean Power Grid. Putting these commitments into practice requires clearer emergency supply-sharing arrangements, coordinated stockpile planning and investment in cross-border electricity connections.

Regional cooperation must be matched by support for households when prices spike. Governments should prepare targeted transfers and protect affordable transport and basic services before a crisis forces them into improvised relief.

Europe’s governments must maintain order while protecting the right to peaceful protest. Their harder task is restoring confidence that economic adjustment will not repeatedly fall on those least able to bear it.

Malaysia and Asean should read these protests as a warning, not a spectacle. Growth, investment and openness remain important, but their political durability depends on whether citizens can see a place for themselves in the prosperity they generate. Economic resilience requires more than sound national accounts. it requires households that can withstand disruption without losing confidence in their future.

* Phar Kim Beng, PhD, is Professor of Asean Studies at the International Islamic University of Malaysia and Director of the Institute of International and Asean Studies (IINTAS), while Dr Vic Li is a Lecturer in East Asian Studies at the University of Sheffield, United Kingdom.

c512df292dc156dd: LOS ANGELES: US-based explorers who travelled to a tiny South Pacific island seeking to conclusively solve the 1937 disappearance of famed aviator Amelia Earhart have determined that an object they suspected was wreckage from her plane was a cluster of washed-up trees.

The mission leaders made the announcement on Monday. The team set out this month from Los Angeles for the archipelago nation of Kiribati on a US$900,000 expedition backed by private donors and Indiana's Purdue University, which has long been associated with Earhart and her legacy.

The objective was to determine whether an elongated, multi-pronged object detected in 2020 satellite imagery in the island's lagoon was a remnant of Earhart's long-missing twin-engine Lockheed Electra 10-E aeroplane.

Such a finding would have decisively supported the hypothesis held by some scholars that Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, crash-landed on or near the coral-ringed atoll and died as castaways there, hundreds of miles from their intended refuelling stop.
'Adventure is worthwhile'

"Unfortunately, we weren't able to find that smoking gun," Purdue general counsel and team member Steve Schultz said in a video message recorded on the island of Nikumaroro, part of the Phoenix Islands in Kiribati.
Quoting Earhart, he added: "You know, Amelia herself said, 'Adventure is worthwhile in itself.'"

After a week on the island, the team ultimately concluded that the "visual anomaly" detected by satellite "was likely a collection of large trees" wedged in the lagoon's sand, the expedition said in a statement.

Much of the debris had fragmented and washed away since it was first spotted, leaving a smaller Y-shaped segment whose reflective surface — suggestive of metal — turned out to come from "its carbonate veneer", the team said.

Two previous attempts to locate the aircraft's wreckage in the ocean around Nikumaroro also proved fruitless, while a plane-shaped sonar image captured elsewhere on the sea floor turned out to be a pile of rocks.

Earhart and Noonan were last seen taking off in the Electra on July 2, 1937, from Papua New Guinea, during Earhart's multi-stage attempt to become the first woman to pilot an aeroplane around the world and the first aviator to circumnavigate the equator.
Radio contact with the flight was lost the next day after Earhart, 39, reported that "gas is running low", followed by her final known transmission giving her navigational line of position.
Castaway hypothesis 'remains very strong'
The disappearance prompted one of the largest air-sea searches ever undertaken and remains one of the great unsolved mysteries of the 20th century and aviation history.

The expedition's leader, Richard Pettigrew, head of the Archaeological Legacy Institute in Eugene, Oregon, said evidence supporting the "castaway hypothesis" — that Earhart and Noonan died while marooned on Nikumaroro — "remains very strong".

He cited evidence collected over more than 30 years by veteran Earhart explorer Ric Gillespie, co-founder of The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery and author of the 2024 book One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy.

Gillespie's case includes multiple radio distress calls picked up in the days immediately after Earhart vanished, with bearings converging on Nikumaroro, and a 2018 forensic analysis of human bones recovered on the island in 1940 that found they belonged to a woman of Earhart's build and stature.

Gillespie's investigation also encompassed artefacts found on the island, including a woman's shoe, a compact case, a freckle cream jar and a medicine vial, all dating to the 1930s, as well as remnants of a jackknife similar to one Earhart carried on the plane.
Another piece of evidence is a photograph taken of the island's shoreline months after Earhart vanished, showing an object that appears to be the Electra's landing gear.
The Purdue expedition said this month that it had uncovered several other artefacts, including a 30-inch-long steel tube found in the lagoon, that could yield further evidence when studied.
According to Gillespie, the plane has been lost to history, eventually swept by tides off the coral flat where it had landed and carried into the sea, where it sank and broke apart in the surf.

The official US government view of Earhart's fate has long been that her plane ran out of fuel and crashed at sea near its intended refuelling destination of Howland Island, another small island about 640km northwest of Nikumaroro.

f96fb85e64ed4d23: FRANCE'S worst bout of civil unrest in years has plunged President Emmanuel Macron's final months in office deeper into turmoil, exposing the powerlessness of a leader struggling to contain social anger with little money to spend, scant political capital and an increasingly fragile grip on public order.

The rioting that swept across France on Saturday, leaving a trail of looted shops, torched buildings and defaced public institutions, presents Macron with perhaps the most explosive challenge of his twilight presidency: a country demanding more from a state that can no longer afford to give much.
Macron came to power almost a decade ago promising to upend France's sclerotic political class, turbocharge economic reforms and restore authority through a more assertive presidency.

Instead, with just six months left in office, he finds himself effectively a lame-duck head of state presiding over a country mired in political paralysis, facing acute financial pressures and grappling with unrest that has exposed the limits of state authority.

Unlike during the Yellow Vest uprising of 2018-2019, when Macron sought to defuse public anger with billions of euros in concessions, France's strained public finances and fractured parliament leave him with precious few levers to pull.
Even former allies are now openly scathing, tracing the country's current impasse to Macron's decision to call a snap parliamentary election in 2024 that weakened his authority.
"The end of this term is a slow agony," said Loïc Kervran, a former lawmaker from Macron's camp, on X.
"The president paralysed the country with his absurd decision to dissolve parliament in 2024. Arguably the worst decision in the history of the Fifth Republic."

The turmoil may benefit far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, who is already the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race and stands to gain from both the anger over declining living standards and the fears over law and order unleashed by the weekend's violence.
"Le Pen no longer needs to spend any money to campaign," Jean-Baptiste Moreau, another former Macron lawmaker, told Reuters. "It's not just a clear path ahead of her — it's a six-lane highway."
Le Pen delivered her own message to the nation in a video statement on Sunday, portraying Macron's administration as a crumbling power and casting herself as the figure capable of restoring order.
When Macron later addressed the country, he offered little concrete action, stopping short of declaring a state of emergency.
Opponents and one-time allies alike were underwhelmed. His former prime minister, Edouard Philippe, now preparing his own presidential run, was unsparing in his criticism.
"Mr President, I listened to you last night," he wrote on X. "I would have preferred, like millions of French people, decisions and initiatives to restore order."

But even Philippe is struggling to shake off his past association with Macron, and most recent polls show far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon edging ahead of him in the race to qualify for the second-round runoff vote.
That outcome would all but guarantee a Le Pen victory, according to opinion polls.

Investors also took fright. Market analysts say the violence adds another layer of political risk at a time when France is already under scrutiny over its swelling debt burden and struggle to reduce one of the euro zone's largest budget deficits.
The president now finds himself trapped between bond markets demanding spending restraint and protesters demanding the opposite.

Despite calls from opponents to remain in France, Macron arrived in Kuwait on Monday on a Gulf tour he says will help secure fuel supplies and ease some of the economic pressures that have helped swell the ranks of the protesters.
The trip carries risks, reinforcing perceptions of a president disconnected from the public mood.

Images of Macron attending a Celine Dion concert with his wife Brigitte on Friday evening, hours before the unrest erupted, prompted ridicule on social media and became an easy symbol for critics seeking to portray him as detached from events.
Moreau, who spoke to Macron on Sunday, said he urged him to prepare an orderly early departure to break the current political deadlock and avoid another six months of drift.
"He doesn't want to give up, that's not his character. But that's what he should do for the country," he said.
* The writer is from Reuters

1a5e3014c944b911: PARIS, Oct 20 — France announced partial curfews in Paris and other cities on Monday after weekend demonstrations over soaring prices degenerated into some of the worst street violence in recent years.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu did not rule out imposing a state of emergency after the interior minister said police had “lost control”.

Tourists in Paris had a taste of the disruption on Monday when they found the Louvre closed because of a small group of student protesters, while the US embassy in Paris urged American citizens to avoid the demonstrations.
Facing accusations that it failed to anticipate and respond to the violence, the government has vowed to re-establish order, while officials scrambled to contain public anger.
The unrest, erupting just six months before France elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron, threatened to continue, with organisers calling for a new round of protests next Saturday.
Authorities said partial curfews would be enforced from Monday evening to Tuesday morning in a number of cities including Paris, Lille and Lyon, to protect businesses.
In the capital, a curfew was ordered from 11.00pm (6.00am Malaysian time), while demonstrations were banned from 8.00pm.
“I’m absolutely determined to restore public order,” Lecornu said.
Other European countries have also seen demonstrations over rising prices, with smaller clashes breaking out in Milan and Belgium over the weekend and protests simmering in Spain and Portugal.

Some half a million people turned out across France on Saturday to denounce the surging cost of living, a culmination of four weeks of protests that began with students demanding better conditions at high schools.

What started as peaceful demonstrations descended into violence in many cities, as masked groups attacked law enforcement, broke into public buildings and set some ablaze, looted shops, and set fire to cars, bicycles and scooters.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Protesters near Chatelet in central Paris on October 18, 2026. — AFP pic
Listings for ‘stolen goods’

On Monday, France’s digital minister, Anne Le Henanff, urged online resale platforms to remove listings for “stolen items” following Saturday’s looting and summoned representatives of companies including Vinted and eBay.
After the weekend scenes of chaos, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez offered his resignation, but Macron refused to accept it.
More than 2,500 people were arrested and nearly 1,000 members of the security forces injured. Protesters were also hurt, with one demonstrator’s hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade.
Macron acknowledged failures in the government response, which had seen 60,000 law enforcement personnel deployed on Saturday.

Nationwide, more than 2,513 people have been taken into police custody since the weekend, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said. He added that 67 had been jailed and “dozens” of criminal cases opened.
Darmanin also said authorities would use facial recognition on social media to identify perpetrators.
At least 3,000 shops were damaged, with the cost running into hundreds of millions of euros.
In an address to the nation Sunday, Macron slammed the “unbridled” violence.
The European Union called the violence “unacceptable” but warned that the right to peaceful protest “must be protected” in France.
Germany condemned the violence and updated its travel advice for France, saying “further outbreaks of violence in the coming days cannot be ruled out”.
China has warned citizens travelling to France to be aware of risks and take safety precautions, state broadcaster CCTV reported.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A looted shop in Lille. — AFP pic
Louvre blocked
In Paris on Monday, a dozen demonstrators blocked the entrance to the Louvre, the most visited museum in the world, while bewildered tourists looked on.
“We don’t want to get involved. We want to stand back and get away from them,” Pat Boland, a tourist from Australia, said of the protests.
The pensioner, 73, spoke to AFP outside barricades that had been erected at the Louvre, which was closed because a small group of protesters stood by its famed glass pyramid entrance.
The unrest has flared before presidential elections in April and May that will elect a new French president after a decade of centrist Macron.
Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate, is riding high in the polls.
The government has accused ultra-left groups of stoking the violence to boost the chances of the far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon in the presidential polls.
The interior minister and intelligence services were to meet late Monday to discuss the violence.
Europe
During the weekend, clashes broke out on the sidelines of a cost-of-living demonstration in Milan.
“I’m very worried because it’s a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself,” mayor Giuseppe Sala said.
In Belgium, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in Brussels and Liege.
In Spain protesters have set up tents in the heart of Madrid to denounce soaring housing costs, with similar encampments going up in neighbouring Portugal’s main cities of Lisbon and Porto. — AFP

bc8b2005bd49238e: SINGAPORE: The US dollar traded in a narrow range in early Asian trading on Tuesday as a tentative recovery in investor confidence supported higher-yielding currencies, while rising political risks in Europe continued to unsettle markets.

The euro was steady at US$1.1216, while the British pound rose 0.1 per cent to US$1.3308. The Australian dollar gained 0.1 per cent to US$0.6986, while the New Zealand dollar edged up 0.1 per cent to US$0.5668.
Against the yen, the US dollar was flat at 158.56 yen ahead of an auction of 20-year Japanese government bonds.
"FX markets reflected the improvement in risk appetite, with higher-carry currencies finding buyers," Pepperstone Group head of research Chris Weston said.

"Europe was less convincing," Weston said. "French sovereign risk is clearly being priced into European equities, but the euro's resilience suggests traders aren't yet treating it as a systemic European problem."
French authorities imposed curfews in several cities on Monday after nationwide anti-government protests plunged President Emmanuel Macron's final months in office into turmoil.
In Italy, the government said it would deploy 500 troops following two days of unrest.
"The spread of French government bonds over Germany has come under renewed widening pressure against the backdrop of violent protests grabbing the headlines," ING analysts said in a client note.
"Tuesday will likely see more headlines around the 2027 budget, as (the French) Parliament is slated for a first formal vote on the revenue section of the finance bill."
The spread between French and German 10-year government bonds widened 9.9 basis points on Monday to 147.3 basis points. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was flat at 5.131 per cent.
The US dollar index, which measures the greenback against six major currencies, ended a two-day losing streak on Monday, rising 0.2 per cent to 101.98.
Against the Chinese yuan, the US dollar was flat at 6.6811 yuan in offshore trading after the People's Bank of China kept interest rates unchanged, in line with market expectations.
Bitcoin was flat at US$81,906.58, while ether edged up 0.3 per cent to US$2,405.99.
02e34f7ad02fa29e: SUNGAI SIPUT: Eighteen oil palm smallholders in Rancangan Tanah Belia Khas (RTBK) Kampung Perlop 1 here are facing mounting distress after a herd of wild elephants destroyed their crops spanning about 81 hectares since early September.
One of the affected smallholders, Mastura Yusuf, 65, said her 12.1-ha plot suffered severe damage, with over 300 oil palm trees destroyed, particularly three-year-old saplings.
Mastura, who has been farming the land since 2002, said it was the worst destruction she had experienced from continuous elephant attacks.
She said the wild elephants also damaged farm infrastructure, including water storage containers and concrete water tanks.
She added that the intrusions not only threatened the main source of income for her and fellow villagers, but also ruined repeated replanting efforts.
She said the elephant intrusions had become increasingly frequent this year, particularly in September and October, forcing her to bear replanting costs for four separate cycles.
"If it costs RM35 just to plant a single tree, you can imagine how much loss I have suffered, not including other costs such as worker wages, fertiliser, and pesticides.
"We noticed the elephant attacks starting last year, but they have become more frequent recently, especially at night," she said when met at the plantation yesterday.
Another smallholder, Muhammad Azlan Adnan, 42, said two hectares of his six-hectare oil palm plot suffered extensive damage, particularly to the shoots and leaves.

"For smaller trees, the impact is worse because once pulled by an elephant, the tree dies instantly. Based on tracks, footprint sizes, and dung left behind, there are probably two or three elephants that entered my farm," he said.

Meanwhile, Mohd Faiz Ahmad, 40, said 120 out of 550 oil palm trees on his land were trampled and uprooted, resulting in losses between RM16,000 and RM17,000 in land preparation, pesticides, fertiliser, and replanting costs.
He said the severe disruption left most smallholders drained of capital and demoralised from continuing maintenance work for upcoming crops.
"Therefore, we appeal for intervention and financial assistance from relevant government agencies to ease our financial burden," he said.
d390c7df2625223a: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 20 — Malaysia aims to equip at least 50 per cent of its 34 expressways with Smart Highway technology to enhance road safety, improve traffic flow and boost transport system efficiency.

Works Minister Datuk Seri Alexander Nanta Linggi said the initiative would incorporate artificial intelligence (AI), smart closed-circuit television (CCTV) systems, and detection and early-warning systems for high-risk incidents, including accidents.
Other features include solar-powered lighting, digital mobility applications and electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure.

“Malaysia is also prioritising the development of a National Intelligent Traffic Management Centre (NITMC) to strengthen real-time monitoring, integrated data analysis and traffic management coordination.

“Another key component is the Multi-Lane Free Flow (MLFF) toll collection system, which allows vehicles to pass through toll plazas without stopping at barriers, thereby reducing congestion and saving travel time,” he said in a statement issued by the Ministry of Works (KKR) yesterday.

Nanta highlighted the initiative during his address at a high-level roundtable session held in conjunction with the 2026 Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) World Congress in Gangneung, South Korea, from October 19 to 23.

Themed “Beyond Mobility, Connected World”, the congress brings together about 60,000 participants from around 90 countries to discuss innovations and future developments in intelligent transport systems.

On the implementation of the initiatives, Nanta said the government was allowing highway concessionaires and industry partners to refine a business-to-business (B2B) model under the regulatory oversight of the Malaysian Highway Authority (MHA).
He said the approach took into account technological and commercial viability, system interoperability, payment integration, data security and consumer protection.
“The current focus is on finalising the technical, operational and legal preparations before the proposal is submitted to the government for consideration and final approval,” the statement said.

Meanwhile, Nanta held a bilateral meeting with the Republic of Korea’s Second Vice-Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, Jeong Eui-kyung, to strengthen cooperation in infrastructure development, construction technology and intelligent transport systems.

Speaking to the Malaysian media after the meeting, Nanta said both countries discussed ways to enhance cooperation in road and highway infrastructure development, including the adoption of new technologies and more efficient management methods.
He said the meeting also reviewed progress in implementing cooperation under a memorandum of understanding (MoU) previously signed between the MHA and the Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC).

“During the bilateral meeting, we reviewed what has been achieved and discussed how cooperation between the two countries could be further strengthened, particularly in the road and highway development industry and the application of the latest technologies and methods,” he said.

Nanta added that the collaboration would continue, with the MHA and KEC scheduled to hold a follow-up session today to further strengthen their partnership in highway infrastructure development. — Bernama
b43886b1179d1eb0: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 20 — Opposition leader Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainudin expects Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim to call the 16th general election by August next year, citing growing tensions between Pakatan Harapan and Umno, according to Free Malaysia Today (FMT).

Speaking in an interview with BFM Radio, Hamzah said the unity government might struggle to remain intact beyond 2027, pointing to renewed scrutiny of Umno president Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s court cases by PH lawmakers.
Hamzah, who leads Wawasan, suggested that the growing friction between the two political blocs could prompt Anwar to call an election before the coalition government fractures.
“I think they have already started to break up. So he has to call (for an election) before that,” he was quoted as saying.

The Attorney-General’s Chambers decided in January to take no further action on 47 charges involving corruption, criminal breach of trust and money laundering against Zahid, who is also Barisan Nasional chairman.
The decision drew criticism from DAP leaders, FMT reported.
Hamzah also suggested Anwar could capitalise on the 2027 SEA Games to build public support before calling an election immediately after the sporting event, scheduled for September 18 to 29.
“Whether it will happen or not, I don’t know. I’m not very sure about that,” he said, as reported by FMT.

He also pointed to the 2027 Budget, which he said contained numerous benefits for the public, as well as a substantial increase in funding for the Election Commission, as possible indications that a general election was approaching.
The EC’s allocation under the recently tabled 2027 Budget rose to RM367 million, compared with RM167 million allocated the previous year.
The next general election must be held by February 2028. Anwar said last month that he was open to considering calls for an early election.
603dbcb3fa89fbc5: KUANTAN, Oct 20 — Police have crippled four gangs suspected of robbing and stealing cables belonging to the East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) and Telekom Malaysia (TM) in operations conducted from October 12 until yesterday around Temerloh and Mentakab.

Temerloh police chief ACP Mohd Nasyim Bahron said in a statement that between September and October this year, two robbery cases at ECRL cable storage facilities and five TM cable theft cases were reported around Temerloh, Mentakab, and Lanchang.
He said 17 local men aged between 20 and 60 were arrested during the operations, with total losses incurred by ECRL and TM estimated at RM75,000.

“The first group, known as Geng Ravi, was crippled through operations from October 12 to October 15. Investigations revealed the gang is also believed to be involved in several iron and cable theft cases at project sites and factories abandoned by their owners since July this year, while police are tracking down two other suspects who remain at large,” he said.

Meanwhile, he said on October 14, police crippled Geng Kepala, believed to be involved in several Tenaga Nasional Berhad cable thefts at storage facilities, factories, and roadsides around Mentakab since August.

Mohd Nasyim said police arrested a 28-year-old man believed to be a member of Geng Dany in Mentakab yesterday for suspected TM cable theft, adding the gang was previously active in similar activities around Kuala Lumpur.
“The suspect confessed to involvement in several TM cable thefts along roadsides around Mentakab since October this year, alongside another accomplice still at large,” he said.

In an early-morning operation yesterday, he said the department crippled Geng Mista, believed to have been involved in several TM cable thefts from manholes and roadside poles around Temerloh, Mentakab, Jerantut, and Maran since July.
“The gang leader was identified as a member of Geng Kepala arrested on October 14, while another suspect remains at large,” he said.

He said police seized several vehicles, including a lorry, along with coils and cut cable pieces belonging to ECRL, TNB, and TM. They also seized cut iron pole pieces and tools believed to have been used to steal and process cables.

Mohd Nasyim said all suspects were detained to assist in investigations under Section 395 and Section 379 of the Penal Code, Section 431A of the Penal Code, and Section 235(2) of the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998. — Bernama

35b3e51ca792d33f: TASEK GELUGOR, Oct 20 — Police have detained a babysitter to assist in investigations into the death of a 10-month-old baby boy who was reported to have died while in the woman’s care here yesterday.
Seberang Perai Utara district police chief ACP Anuar Abdul Rahman said the woman was detained following the incident and the case is being investigated under Section 31(1)(a) of the Child Act 2001.
“Investigations are ongoing, and we are waiting for the post-mortem report to find out the actual cause of the baby’s death,” he said in a statement last night.
It is understood that the baby’s mother sent him to the babysitter early this morning.
The 25-year-old babysitter allegedly found the baby weak and lethargic at about 9.50 am and took him to a nearby clinic.
The baby is believed to have died before arriving at the clinic. Preliminary physical examinations reportedly found no visible bruising on his body. — Bernama
aa53fa485587a481: BUTTERWORTH, Oct 20 — Police have detained six men to assist investigations into the abuse of an Indonesian woman in Tanjong Sepat, Selangor, in a raid at a business premise at Pusat Perniagaan Oren, Jalan Merbau, here today.

Seberang Perai Utara district police chief ACP Anuar Abdul Rahman said the 6.30pm raid was carried out by the Selangor police contingent headquarters (IPK) Criminal Investigation Department (CID) team, with assistance from the Penang IPK CID team.
